newsitem.title: ITALY: Car incentives boost Italy's industrial output.
newsitem.headline: Car incentives boost Italy's industrial output.

text.p: Italian industrial output jumped by more than expected in April, fuelled by a government car incentive scheme, but economists warned on Friday that the recovery could run out of steam later in the year.

Figures released in Rome by national statistics institute Istat on Friday showed that industrial output surged by a seasonally adjusted 0.7 percent in April, well ahead of forecasts of a 0.3 percent rise.
The industrial production index had risen by a revised 0.6 percent in March on a seasonally adjusted basis.
Unadjusted, the index rose 8.2 percent after shrinking by an unadjusted 3.7 percent in March 1997.
"As we expected the recovery is being heavily influenced by car sales on the back of the incentive scheme," said Maria Rosa Trolese, an economist at Deutsche Bank in Milan.
"The problem is how long can this recovery last?" she added.

Istat said average daily output, non seasonally adjusted but adjusted to take account of the number of workdays in the month, rose 3.9 percent year-on-year in April after a revised rise of 0.2 percent in March.
Production of consumer goods, on an unadjusted basis, rose 12.3 percent year-on-year in April. Output of investment goods rose 2.9 percent and intermediate goods rose 8.1 percent.
The Transport Ministry said on Tuesday that new car registrations had jumped 43.23 percent in May from a year earlier.
National new car registrations rose to 232,600 vehicles in May, compared with 162,399 in May 1996. In April the national market showed a record 52.57 percent rise from year-ago levels.

The car market has been driven higher by a government-backed new car buying incentive which started in January and offers price discounts to owners of cars which are more than 10 years old who trade them in for new ones.
The scheme is due to end at the end of September but the chairman of Italian car producer Fiat, Cesare Romiti, called for the incentives to be phased out gradually.
French car sales have fallen sharply this year as weak demand persisted more than six months after the end of a similar national car-buying incentive scheme.

Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio signalled on Thursday that he would be reluctant to cut interest rates -- despite calls repeated calls for cheaper borrowing costs from industrialists and politicians -- unless the government stepped up efforts to cut public spending.
Fazio said he did not want to give the economy an artificial shot in the arm "Don't ask me to force the economy or to drug it," he said.
